approachQuestion.prompt:
Parity signature spans. A log stores n nonnegative integer bit masks. Count nonempty contiguous intervals whose bitwise XOR equals target. Return one count.

Input: masks=[1,2,3], target=3. Output: 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ masks[i],target < 2^20. XOR and arithmetic on these integers take constant time; answer fits 64 bits.

Which approach handles the complete task correctly and efficiently?

options.text: Maintain running XOR X and a frequency map seeded with 0:1. At each element add the prior frequency of X XOR target to the answer, then increment frequency[X].
options.feedback: XOR cancels equal earlier bits, so two boundary XORs yield target exactly when the earlier value equals X XOR target.

options.text: Use the frequency of X-target instead of X XOR target.
options.feedback: For [1,2], target 2, the ending XOR is 3: subtraction searches for 1 and happens to work here; for [2,1], target 1, it searches for 2 correctly, but [3,1], target 1 ends at 2 and searches for 1 instead of the earlier 3, missing [1].

options.text: Enumerate every interval and update its XOR as the right endpoint moves.
options.feedback: This gives correct results, but repeatedly traverses overlapping candidates. The selected summary reuses their shared work.

feedback.reason: Maintain running XOR X and a frequency map seeded with 0:1. At each element add the prior frequency of X XOR target to the answer, then increment frequency[X].
details: Maintain running XOR X and a frequency map seeded with 0:1. At each element add the prior frequency of X XOR target to the answer, then increment frequency[X].

XOR is its own inverse: earlierPrefix XOR currentPrefix equals target exactly when earlierPrefix=currentPrefix XOR target. Subtraction is the wrong inverse here. Query before insertion to avoid a zero-length interval.

“Maintain running XOR X and a frequency map seeded with 0:1. At each element add the prior frequency of X XOR target to the answer, then increment frequency[X].”: XOR cancels equal earlier bits, so two boundary XORs yield target exactly when the earlier value equals X XOR target.

“Use the frequency of X-target instead of X XOR target.”: For [1,2], target 2, the ending XOR is 3: subtraction searches for 1 and happens to work here; for [2,1], target 1, it searches for 2 correctly, but [3,1], target 1 ends at 2 and searches for 1 instead of the earlier 3, missing [1].
“Enumerate every interval and update its XOR as the right endpoint moves.”: This gives correct results, but repeatedly traverses overlapping candidates. The selected summary reuses their shared work.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the method in the reveal. Choose its tightest expected-time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. Hash lookup and insertion take expected constant time including amortized resizing, without worst-case guarantees. Include the map, exclude input and scalar result; no recursion or input copy.

options.text: Expected O(n) time; O(n) auxiliary space
Worst-case O(n) time; O(n) auxiliary space
Expected O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Expected O(n²) time; O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: One XOR update and expected-cost frequency lookup occur per entry.
details: A constant number of expected constant-time hash operations per element gives expected O(n) time. At most n+1 keys require O(n) space.
Hash lookup and insertion take expected constant time including amortized resizing, without worst-case guarantees. Include the map, exclude input and scalar result; no recursion or input copy.

One XOR update and a bounded number of expected-amortized map lookups/increments are performed per element, giving expected O(n) total time under the stated hash model. The available worst-case-linear option strengthens that assumption without justification. Summing stored frequencies counts matching intervals without enumerating all O(n²) endpoint pairs.

The map may store a distinct prefix XOR at every boundary, up to n+1 keys, so auxiliary space is O(n). The expected-linear/constant-space option omits this map. The quadratic/constant-space option describes a different interval-enumeration strategy, not the fixed map method. Supplied masks and the returned scalar count are excluded; prefix-map storage is included.
